column1: # Register of option priorities — read by scripts/check-option-priorities.sh
#   watch  <full option path>  <file that writes it>  <note>
#   allow  <full option path>  <upstream module>  <why the collision is harmless>
# `count` rows exist so a priority cannot be added without a ruling: the seal
# compares them against the source and fails on any drift.
# `watch` rows list the THIRD-PARTY options STC writes with mkDefault — the only
# ones that can collide with an upstream module. Options under stc.* cannot, so
# they are not watched. The full path is here because a grep cannot infer it from
# The rule these rows serve is in docs/*/reference/overridable-defaults.md.

column6: three GUI relics as defaults so one terminal can be dropped; pinentry at mkOverride 900 to beat enginseer's default without beating the consumer
tool settings are the consumer's taste, not the profile's trade; the tool list itself stays at normal priority
socketProxy, crowdsec and preSwitchChecks are additive; autoPrune is a default kept off because a missed weekly window takes the stack down; serverSurvivability is additive
networking and the hardening suite are additive; zfs, impermanence and aws stay at normal priority because this profile declares the filesystems that assume them; serverSurvivability is additive
the profile is named for what it does, not the GPU or audio stack it assumes
the six sub-relics are independent and nothing here assumes any one of them
pipewire is additive; plasma6 stays pinned because it is the profile's subject
networking and hardening additive; the mkForce block is an image builder having the last word on its own boot layout, over STC's own boot relic; serverSurvivability is additive

the serial getty must yield to a nixosTest claiming ttyS0; udisks2 documents an intent upstream already defaults to false
firmware that refuses EFI variable writes, and chroot installs, need canTouchEfiVariables false
log rotation policy belongs to the operator; files, frequency, rotate and postrotate stay pinned because they are wired to this relic
mkForce on /tmp because the relic replaces whatever the hardware configuration or disko declared for it with a tmpfs
an operator must be able to re-enable core dumps for one crash; read the warning on the relic's doc page before doing it
hideMounts only changes what mount shows, so an operator debugging persistence can turn it off
predictable interface names are a proposal; useDHCP moved to an option after this seal measured a collision with networking.ifstate
xserver.enable as a default, without which the relic's own documented wayland = false option is unreachable
emergency mode, the generation cap, the watchdog timeout and the sleep ban are policy a consumer with console access, a larger ESP or a flaky watchdog may want otherwise
mkForce throughout is this relic's entire job — neutralising secrets, pools and images — and it only ever writes inside virtualisation.vmVariant
forceImportRoot/All stay false but reachable: a pool legitimately carrying a foreign hostid is a real one-off need
